title: Hebrews 13:7–17
context: The readers are to remember their former leaders and imitate their faith, because Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. They should not be carried away by strange teachings about foods, since the heart is strengthened by grace. Believers have an altar the old priests cannot share. As Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people by his blood, so believers should go to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach, seeking the city to come. They are to offer a sacrifice of praise and do good, and to obey their present leaders, who watch over their souls. Both traditions draw rich teaching here, with differences on the sacraments and church order.

verses.text: Remember your leaders, men who spoke to you the word of God, and considering the results of their conduct, imitate their faith.
verses.arminianNotes: Remember your leaders who spoke God’s word to you; imitate their faith. Arminian readers see faithful examples encouraging believers to persevere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see godly leaders as a gift of God for the church’s edification.

verses.text: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever. Both traditions treasure this verse as an affirmation of Christ’s unchanging nature. Arminian readers see his constant faithfulness to all who come to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s immutability as the security of his people.

verses.text: Don’t be carried away by various and strange teachings, for it is good that the heart be established by grace, not by foods, through which those who were so occupied were not benefited.
verses.arminianNotes: Do not be led away by strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods. Arminian readers see grace, not ritual, as the strength of the believer.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see grace strengthening the heart, in contrast with ceremonial observances.

verses.text: We have an altar from which those who serve the holy tabernacle have no right to eat.
verses.arminianNotes: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. Arminian readers see Christ’s sacrifice as the believer’s altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the altar as the cross. They reject reading it as a sacrificial altar for the Mass.

verses.text: For the bodies of those animals, whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as an offering for sin, are burned outside of the camp.
verses.arminianNotes: The bodies of animals whose blood was brought into the holy place were burned outside the camp. Arminian readers see the sin offering as a picture of Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Day of Atonement fulfilled in Christ.

verses.text: Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside of the gate.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus also suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood. Arminian readers see Christ’s blood available to sanctify all who come to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Christ’s blood actually sanctifying “the people,” those he represents.
verses.keyContrast: Both see Jesus sanctifying the people through his blood. Arminian readers see that sanctification offered to all and received by faith. Reformed readers see it effectively accomplished for those Christ represents.

verses.text: Let’s therefore go out to him outside of the camp, bearing his reproach.
verses.arminianNotes: Let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. Arminian readers see a call to costly identification with Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see believers leaving behind the old system to follow Christ.

verses.text: For we don’t have here an enduring city, but we seek that which is to come.
verses.arminianNotes: Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come. Arminian readers see pilgrim faith seeking the heavenly city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the believer’s hope fixed on the city God has prepared.

verses.text: Through him, then, let’s offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name.
verses.arminianNotes: Through him let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God. Arminian readers see praise as the fitting response of grateful believers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see praise as the believer’s priestly sacrifice, offered through Christ.

verses.text: But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.
verses.arminianNotes: Do not neglect to do good and share, for such sacrifices please God. Arminian readers see good works as pleasing to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see good works as pleasing to God through Christ, not as meriting salvation.

verses.text: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch on behalf of your souls, as those who will give account, that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be unprofitable for you.
verses.arminianNotes: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account. Arminian readers see leaders helping believers persevere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see church leaders as shepherds appointed by Christ, who will give account to him.
